extraction_text: Arjuna broke through the armies of Drona and Bhoja to kill King Jayadratha.
Arjuna killed Prince Sudakshina of the Kambojas and the brave Vinda.
Duryodhana went to Drona after his army collapsed.
Duryodhana pleaded with Drona to protect King Jayadratha from Arjuna.
Duryodhana accused Drona of favoring the Pandavas despite receiving benefits from the Kauravas.
Duryodhana expressed regret for preventing King Jayadratha from returning home based on Drona's promise.
Drona assured Duryodhana he would speak truthfully and not take offense, treating him like his own son Ashvatthama.
Drona explained Arjuna's speed and prowess, attributing it to Krishna's charioteering and his own old age.
Duryodhana expresses his vow to capture Yudhishthira in front of all archers.
Duryodhana explains he abandoned his position at the battlefront to not pursue Arjuna because Yudhishthira is now before him.
Duryodhana is encouraged to fight Yudhishthira, who is described as his equal in lineage and achievements.
Duryodhana expresses doubt about his ability to stop Arjuna, citing Arjuna's invincibility and past victories.

attributes.examples: Arjuna defeated Drona, killed Bhishma, Shalya, and hundreds of warriors

extraction_text: Drona assures Duryodhana he will make arrangements so Duryodhana can withstand Arjuna.
Drona performs a ritual with water and mantras to fasten a golden armor on Duryodhana.
Drona declares the armor will make Duryodhana invulnerable to all weapons, even from Krishna, Arjuna, or beings from all three worlds.
Drona invokes blessings from Brahma, all Brahmins, snakes, and royal sages for Duryodhana's protection.

Various deities offer blessings to the king, including Lakshmi, Arundhati, Asita, Devala, Vasistha, Angiras, Bhrigu, Kashyapa, Dhatri, Vidhatri, Skanda, Vivasvat, the elephants of the directions, Earth, sky, atmosphere, planets, and Shesha.
Vritra, son of Tvashtri, displayed his might in battle, defeating thousands of gods, causing them to lose their splendor and strength.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Demon Vritra's power from Tvashtri's penance

extraction_text: The gods, fearful of Vritra, approached Brahma along with Indra seeking refuge.
The gods pleaded with Brahma to save them from Vritra's terror.
Brahma, seeing the gods' despondency, addressed Vishnu and the gods led by Indra, explaining that Vritra was created from Tvashtri's immense penance and had received a boon from Shiva.

Brahma advised the gods to go to Mount Mandara to meet Shiva, describing him as the source of penance, destroyer of Daksha's sacrifice, trident-bearer, lord of all beings, and destroyer of Bhaga's eyes.
Led by Brahma, the gods went to Mount Mandara and saw a heap of splendor like a million suns.
Shiva welcomed the gods and asked what he could do for them, promising their wishes would be fulfilled.
The gods explained that Vritra had taken their splendor, showed their wounded bodies, and sought Shiva's protection.
Shiva acknowledged Vritra's powerful magic from Tvashtri's might and stated it was his duty to help the gods. He gave Indra a golden armor that originated from his own body, along with a mantra.

attributes.supernatural_elements: Armor born from Shiva's body, protective mantra

extraction_text: After receiving the armor and mantra, Indra went to Vritra's army under its protection.

attributes.relationships: Indra empowered by Shiva to confront Vritra

extraction_text: In the great battle, various arrow streams came but could not penetrate the combination of the bandage and armor.
Indra personally killed Vritra in the battle.
Indra gave the charmed bandage and armor to Sage Angiras.
Angiras told his son Brihaspati, who knew spells, about this.
Brihaspati told the wise Sage Agni about it.
Agni gave the armor to Drona.

Drona, with great splendor, spoke gently to Duryodhana and said he would fasten the armor on him with a sacred thread using spells, just as Brahma did for Vishnu in battle and for Indra in the war caused by Indraka.

attributes.supernatural_element: Sacred ritual with spells, historical divine parallels

extraction_text: The Brahmin Drona, following ritual procedures, silently recited spells and fastened the armor on King Duryodhana, sending him to the great battle.

Duryodhana, with great arms, had his armor fastened by the great-souled teacher Drona, led thousands of chariots, Trigarta warriors, thousands of fierce drunk elephants, ten thousand horses, and was surrounded by great chariot warriors.

attributes.forces: Thousands of chariots, Trigarta warriors, drunk elephants, horses

extraction_text: Duryodhana advanced toward Arjuna's chariot, with various musical instruments playing, like Bali, son of Virochana.
Seeing Duryodhana, descendant of Kuru, depart, like a bottomless ocean beginning to surge, shouts arose in your army.
Arjuna, son of Pritha, and Krishna, descendant of Vrishni, both rushed in, with the bull among men Duryodhana chasing behind.

attributes.relationship: Arjuna and Krishna are allies, Duryodhana is enemy

extraction_text: With great noise, the Pandavas and Somakas quickly charged toward Drona, and the battle began.
The battle between the Panchalas and Kurus in front of the armies was cruel, fierce, hair-raising, and a miracle, unseen and unheard before, occurring with the sun at the sky's center.
The army of the sons of Pritha, led by Dhrishtadyumna, arranged in array, warriors together showered arrow rain on Drona's army.
Our side, with the warrior chief Drona at the forefront, also poured arrow rain on the sons of Pritha led by Dhrishtadyumna, grandson of Drupada.

The two chariot-equipped armies were spectacular, like two huge clouds driven by opposing winds approaching each other at winter's end, meeting with great force like the Ganga and Yamuna rivers in monsoon, with armies as clouds, elephants, horses, and chariots as elements, maces as lightning, weapons as wind, and Drona as a gale bringing thousands of arrow streams to the Pandava army's fire.
Drona (the Brahmin chief) disrupted the Pandava army like a hurricane disturbing the sea at summer's end.
The Pandavas attacked Drona with full force, trying to break through like floodwaters against a dam.
Drona resisted the angry Pandavas, Panchalas, and Kekayas like a mountain holding back tides.
Other kings and heroes surrounded and blocked the Panchalas from all sides.
Dhrishtadyumna (grandson of Drupada) led the Pandavas in repeated attacks against Drona, trying to break enemy formation.
Drona and Dhrishtadyumna exchanged arrow showers in battle.
Dhrishtadyumna was compared to a massive cloud, with swords as wind, spears/javelins/double-edged swords as rain, bowstrings as lightning, and bow sounds as thunder.

attributes.supernatural_element: Extended metaphor of warrior as storm cloud

extraction_text: Dhrishtadyumna's arrow streams and stone showers killed many chariot warriors and horses, enveloping the entire army.
Whenever Drona attacked any chariot group with arrows, Dhrishtadyumna diverted him with arrows.
Despite Drona's fierce fighting, his army split into three groups when approaching Dhrishtadyumna.
Some warriors retreated to Bhoja king, some to Shalya, and some joined Drona under Pandava attack.
Drona reorganized his army, but Dhrishtadyumna scattered them again.
The Kaurava army split into three groups and suffered slaughter from Pandavas and Srinjayas like unprotected cattle hunted by beasts.
Death seemed to be devouring warriors confused by Dhrishtadyumna's attacks.
The Pandavas repeatedly attacked the Kaurava army like famine, plague, and robbers afflict a poorly ruled kingdom.
Weapons and armor baked in sunlight, eyes tormented by army-raised dust.
Enraged by his three-split army's slaughter, Drona scattered the Panchalas with arrows.
Drona ravaged and slaughtered the enemy army with arrows, his form like world-ending fire.
Drona shot arrows piercing chariot warriors, horses, elephants, and foot soldiers in succession.
No Pandava warrior could withstand Drona's arrows in battle.
Dhrishtadyumna's army became chaotic from both midday sun's heat and Drona's arrows.
Areas swept by Dhrishtadyumna in the Kaurava army looked like forests burned by fire.
Arrows from both Drona and Dhrishtadyumna ravaged both armies, with warriors fighting determinedly.
No warriors from either side showed cowardice or fled the battlefield.
Kunti's son Bhima was surrounded by his cousins Duryodhana, Duhshasana, and the great warrior Vikarna.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, along with the heroic Shamadurti, provided rear support for Duryodhana's three sons.
King Bhagadatta of Pragjyotisha, noble and powerful, led his army and ministers to attack the five sons of Draupadi.
King Shibi's son Nila led a thousand excellent warriors to attack the brave son of the King of Kashi.
King Shalya of Madra surrounded Yudhishthira, who was like a blazing fire.
Duhshasana, impatient, arranged his army and angrily charged at the excellent chariot warrior Satyaki.
Duryodhana, fully armed, led his army and four hundred great archers to attack Shikhandin.
Shakuni led his army and seven hundred Gandhara warriors, armed with bows, spears, arrows, and swords, to attack the son of Madri (Nakula or Sahadeva).
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, risking their lives for their friend, bravely fought King Virata of Matsya on the battlefield.
King Bhagadatta fought vigorously against the invincible Shikhandin, son of Drupada.
King of Avanti led the Shibis and cruel Prabhadrakas to attack Dhrishtadyumna, who was like an embodiment of anger.
Ghatotkacha, a Rakshasa hero, fiercely charged into battle, and Alambusha quickly advanced to confront him.
The great warrior Kuntibhoja led a large army to attack the Rakshasa king Kumbhakarna, who was an embodiment of anger.
King Jayadratha of Sindhu was positioned at the rear of all armies, protected by excellent archers and chariot warriors led by Kripa.
Ashvatthama protected Jayadratha's right wheel, and Karna protected his left wheel.
Warriors led by Vrishasena provided rear guard for Jayadratha, including Kripa, Ghatotkacha, Shala, Shalya, and Dushkarna.
The sons of Pritha (Pandavas) attacked Drona, who guarded the army's entrance, attempting to break through his forces.
Warriors defended their own and Drona's positions, fighting the sons of Pritha on the battlefield, hoping to gain great honor.
Vinda and Anuvinda of Avanti, filled with anger, fought for Duryodhana's benefit and shot ten arrows at Virata.
Virata, undeterred, charged at these two heroic warriors and fought them and their followers.
